newsitem.title: FRANCE: Minicar segment gleams as Mercedes pulls up.
newsitem.headline: Minicar segment gleams as Mercedes pulls up.

text.p: Mercedes-Benz is the last name one expects to find in the cheap-and-cheerful minicar segment, but the prestigious German manufacturer has swerved off course with a tiny model which will be shown in Paris next week.

Ford Motor Co will also display a new minicar at the Paris car show, the Ka. Renault SA will show off a revamped version of its trend-setting Twingo, and Suzuki will introduce the featherweight (730 kg/1,600 lb) Alto.
Mercedes' debut in the so-called A class reflects a renewed interest in minicars among carmakers who had treated the segment as a niche for first-time owners with little money to spend.

Minicars are among the least profitable vehicles for the industry both in terms of profit margins and volumes -- around 600,000 are sold each year in Europe, compared with 3.3 million small cars in the B segment just above.

But manufacturers expect minicar sales in Europe to double or even triple over the next five years, and many are counting on demand for richly-appointed, option-packed versions from a new breed of customers.
"If you look at the demographics in Europe, people are getting older and environmentally sensitive," said analyst Arthur Maher at consulting firm DRI McGraw Hill.
"Cities are more congested. More households have two or three vehicles and they're not looking for something cheap, but rather something affordable, for town travel," he said.
He expects minicar prices to overlap with prices of small cars, which tend to have slightly different characteristics but do not necessarily attract a wealthier customer.
"The market in Europe is not growing very fast, but it is becoming more fragmented. It's more a question of people switching from one niche to another," he said.
"When manufacturers sit down and look at this marketplace, they want to fill every product niche to protect or grow their market share," he said.

Car analysts say the trend toward platform-sharing, that is, building two or more cars on the same platform, has allowed manufacturers to target niches by drastically reducing the development cost of the additional models. The new Ford Ka, for instance, will be built on the same platform as the Fiesta.
Analysts say minicars have become hot because of shifts in other segments of the market, such as the gradual growth in size of small and lower mid-sized cars.
Volkswagen'sGolf, for instance, the leader in the lower mid-sized segment, is larger today than it used to be.
The boom in so-called multi-purpose vehicles has undermined the central position of the stalwart sedan and resulted in more creative combinations for two-car families.
In the past two years, small car sales have gotten an added boost from government incentive schemes in Spain and France that offered rebates to buyers turning in old clunkers.

The incentives boosted demand for little cars just as the French industry was trying to widen its profit margins by moving upmarket. As a result, French carmakers generated fewer additional sales than foreign rivals like Fiat.
"Neither (of the French carmakers) has produced a car in the 40,000-franc category and Fiat has two -- the Punto and the Cinquecento," said analyst John Lawson at Salomon Brothers.
Daimler Benz, which owns Mercedes, has linked up with Swiss Swatchmaker SMH to build the Smart minicar by 1998, and there is talk of Volkswagen turning out a mini Polo.

But the headlong rush to produce tiny cars is not without risk, and Maher worries about carmakers' expectations. He said their minicar production plans assume a market of 1.6 million sales annually within five years, whereas he expects sales over that period to grow to only around 1.2 million.
